items.d: One place to raise an HR request, with routing, SLAs and a visible trail.

detail.thesis:
Employees regularly require support from HR for questions, issues, requests and services that cannot always be completed through standard self-service processes.

When these interactions are handled through a combination of emails, calls, messages, informal follow-ups or basic request tracking, employee support can become difficult to manage consistently as the organization grows.

This creates several business problems:

  • employees may not have one clear place to request HR support and understand what is happening with their request;
  • HR teams may spend significant effort manually following up, forwarding and coordinating requests;
  • ownership of requests may not always be clear;
  • requests may not consistently reach the correct HR team or responsible person;
  • urgent or high-impact issues may be handled in the same way as routine requests;
  • employees may repeatedly contact HR when they do not have clear visibility of progress;
  • service expectations and response commitments may vary between teams or request types;
  • HR teams may have limited visibility of outstanding workload, delays and recurring employee issues; and
  • management may lack measurable information about HR service quality, response times and employee satisfaction.

As employee populations and HR service requirements grow, these challenges can make HR support increasingly dependent on manual coordination and individual follow-up.

The business need is therefore to provide a consistent and measurable way for employees to receive HR support while enabling HR teams to manage service requests with clear ownership, prioritization, communication and accountability.

The existing document already identifies the underlying need for structured handling of inquiries, correct routing, service commitments, ongoing communication and visibility of HR service performance.

items.d: Approve and act on workflow tasks from WhatsApp, without entering PHR.

detail.thesis:
Many HR processes depend on timely action from managers, supervisors and other approvers before the process can continue.

These users are often not frequent HRIS users. Their primary responsibilities sit outside HR administration, and they may only access PHR when a specific employee request or workflow task requires their attention.

This creates a business problem:

HR workflows can remain dependent on people remembering to enter the HR system and complete relatively small actions before the wider business process can continue.

When workflow tasks are not acted on promptly, this can result in:

  • employee requests remaining pending longer than necessary;
  • delays in approvals and other HR processes;
  • bottlenecks where one pending action prevents the next workflow step from starting;
  • HR teams needing to manually remind managers and approvers;
  • employees following up with HR because their request has not progressed;
  • increasing numbers of outstanding approval tasks;
  • slower operational response for time-sensitive HR activities; and
  • reduced effectiveness of workflows that were designed to automate HR processes.

The issue becomes more significant when the approver is a manager or executive who receives many requests but does not regularly work inside PHR.

The business need is therefore to reduce avoidable delays in HR workflows by making it easier for authorized users to respond to workflow tasks at the time those tasks require their attention.

The existing proposal already identifies faster workflow turnaround, fewer pending approvals, reduced bottlenecks and improved operational responsiveness as the expected organizational value.

items.d: Ask workforce questions from Teams, WhatsApp or Google Chat.

detail.thesis:
PHR AI Insights provides conversational workforce analytics, allowing authorized users to ask natural-language questions and receive answers based on the organization's available HR data.

However, the availability of workforce intelligence does not necessarily mean that the people making business decisions are consuming it at the moment those decisions are being made.

Senior leaders such as CEOs, CHROs, CFOs and other management users may require workforce information regularly, but HRIS applications are not always part of their everyday working environment.

This creates a broader business problem:

Workforce intelligence can remain separated from the management conversations and decisions where that intelligence is most valuable.

When a management user needs workforce information, they may have to leave their current working environment, access PHR, navigate to the relevant analytics capability and perform the investigation.

Alternatively, they may depend on HR or another user to retrieve the information for them.

This can result in:

  • slower access to workforce information during management decision making;
  • management decisions being discussed without immediately available HR context;
  • dependency on HR teams to answer analytical questions that the system could potentially answer directly;
  • lower adoption of analytical capabilities among senior users who do not regularly operate within the HRIS;
  • additional effort to move information between PHR and the communication channels where management discussions are taking place; and
  • reduced practical value from the organization's investment in workforce analytics.

At the same time, management users already spend significant portions of their working day within communication and collaboration platforms such as Microsoft Teams, WhatsApp and Google Chat.

items.d: One conversational interface across the whole platform, not another module.

detail.thesis:
As PHR continues to expand, clients are gaining access to more HR capabilities, workflows and configuration options. However, the value of these capabilities depends on users knowing that they exist, knowing where to find them, and understanding how to use the relevant process.

This creates a growing business problem:

The capability of the product can increase faster than the ability of users to consume it.

Employees, managers and HR teams may need to navigate multiple modules and screens, understand different workflows, or depend on training, documentation and experienced users even when their actual business intent is simple — such as applying leave, checking attendance, completing an approval, finding employee information or performing a supervisor activity.

As the platform grows, this can lead to:

  • lower adoption and utilization of capabilities clients already own;
  • increased training, onboarding and support dependency;
  • longer time to complete common HR activities;
  • difficulty discovering functionality already available within PHR;
  • reduced perceived value from the client's HR technology investment; and
  • increasing user experience complexity whenever additional capabilities are introduced.

The opportunity is therefore not simply to provide another AI feature.

It is to create a scalable way for users to access the value already available across PHR without requiring them to understand the structure of the system itself.

items.d: Heavy reports process in the background while light ones stay instant.

detail.thesis:
Reporting is a core part of day-to-day HR and management activities, and users depend on PHR to provide the information they need within a reasonable and predictable timeframe.

As client data volumes, reporting periods and report complexity increase, some reports take significantly longer to generate than others.

This creates a business problem because users cannot always predict how long they will need to wait before the information they requested becomes available.

Long-running report generation can result in:

  • users losing productive time while waiting for reports;
  • uncertainty about whether a report is still processing or has failed;
  • repeated report requests when users are unsure of the processing status;
  • reduced confidence in the reporting experience;
  • difficulty supporting increasingly large client data volumes consistently; and
  • resource-intensive reporting activity potentially affecting the performance and reliability of other PHR operations.

As PHR continues to support larger clients and greater volumes of historical data, this problem is expected to become more significant.

The business need is therefore to ensure that PHR can provide a reliable and scalable reporting experience even when report-processing requirements vary significantly.

items.d: Employee self service through the chat apps people already use.

detail.thesis:
Employees regularly need HR information and services as part of their day-to-day work.

These needs are often relatively simple, such as:

  • checking a leave balance;
  • understanding an HR policy;
  • finding attendance information;
  • checking employee-related information available to them; or
  • completing a common self-service transaction.

However, accessing these services can still require employees to enter the HR system, identify where the relevant capability exists and follow the appropriate process.

For employees who use HR systems only occasionally, this can create unnecessary effort even for simple HR needs.

This creates several business problems:

  • employees may depend on HR teams for information that is already available through self-service;
  • HR teams may repeatedly answer common employee questions;
  • employees may avoid or delay using available self-service capabilities because accessing them feels inconvenient;
  • adoption of digital HR services may remain lower than expected;
  • employees may need to learn different modules, screens and processes for different HR activities;
  • simple HR interactions can take more employee time than necessary; and
  • organizations may not receive the full value from PHR capabilities they have already implemented.

general:
External systems
  • Integrations are built per customer, not offered by the platform. Each one is paid for once rather than holding the account, and a competitor rebuilds the set in a single implementation.

Statutory depth in Payroll and Attendance
  • Statutory rules live in per-customer configuration, not in the platform. Every change is rebuilt account by account, so no customer is safer for being on PeoplesHR.

Platform usage monitoring
  • No account is tagged by which modules it uses or how deeply. We invest on anecdote, and cannot say which modules/capabilities customers use extensively.

Moonshots.note: High risk and high reward bets. Small enough that a failure costs a rounding error, deliberate enough that a success is not an accident.
